title: Leasing Communal Land Needs the Governor's Written Approval
bodyText: Most land in American Samoa is communal (native) family land, controlled by the family's senior matai. A lease of communal land, for any purpose and any tenant, is valid only with the Governor's written approval, may run no longer than 55 years, and until approval is given the signed agreement is only provisional and has no validity. The agreement must state all its terms and go to the Governor with a plan showing where the land is; the Land Commission reviews it first. Within 2 calendar months after approval, the tenant must deposit a properly drawn, attested copy with the Governor's office for confirmation, and it is registered. If you rent a house on communal land, including a house the family has separated from the land by a recorded separation agreement, treat the lease as needing approval unless your lawyer advises otherwise (case law not searched), and use the optional approval clause (`communal-land-lease-approval-as`). Confirm the land's status and who may sign for the family before you sign: a lease of individually owned or freehold land needs no Governor's approval, but it still should be registered (`edu-lease-registration-as`). Disputes over communal land go to the Land and Titles Division, usually only after a hearing before the Secretary of Samoan Affairs. Whatever the land's status, a lease to a corporation (for example an employer renting staff housing) also needs the Governor's written approval and recording before it has any effect (`edu-foreign-ownership-as`).

title: Registering a Written Lease with the Territorial Registrar
bodyText: American Samoa's land law says no instrument passes an interest in land until it is registered with the Territorial Registrar, and a lease is one of the instruments the Registrar registers (the Registrar's fee for registering a land lease or house lease is set by regulation, currently $50). Registration also gives notice of the lease to anyone who later deals with the land. We found no statute saying an unregistered residential lease is unenforceable between landlord and tenant (case law not searched), but registration matters in an eviction: the court rule that lets a tenant stop the eviction by paying the judgment amount within 10 days says it does not apply where no written lease is registered, although the statute on the same point has no such exception (`edu-redemption-after-judgment-as`). Register any written lease, especially one longer than a year or on communal land (where registration follows the Governor's approval, `edu-communal-land-lease-approval-as`). The Registrar may refuse an instrument that appears illegal; a party can ask the High Court to review that decision.

title: Rent Payment Methods in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa law does not tell you which rent payment methods you must accept. We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to take cash or a card, bars you from requiring payment by electronic transfer or an online portal, or limits a fee or surcharge for paying by a particular method. One general rule applies: United States currency is the only legal tender in American Samoa for paying debts. That section does not say a landlord must accept cash when the lease names other methods (case law not searched), so the cautious course is to list the accepted methods in the lease (`acceptable-payment-methods`), keep at least one method that does not depend on the tenant having a bank account or card, and accept cash with a written receipt if a tenant tenders the exact rent in currency. Checks are governed by the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Law, which American Samoa adopted by statute. If you pass on a card processing charge, state it in the lease and keep it to what the processor actually charges you, since the Consumer Protection Act may reach a residential lease.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that bans or regulates setting rents or lease terms with algorithmic pricing or revenue-management software, or that restricts landlords from sharing rent data. We also found no general territorial antitrust law: the only trade-restraint statute in the Code covers shipping by water. Federal antitrust law was not reviewed for this library and may still apply to coordinated pricing, so the cautious course is to set your rents from your own costs and public market information, and not to share nonpublic rent or occupancy data with competing landlords or use a tool that pools it. The one territorial limit on rent levels is the emergency price-gouging rule for month-to-month housing (`edu-rent-control-as`).

title: No Application-Fee Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that caps, bans or regulates a rental application or screening fee, requires you to refund an unused fee, or requires a written notice of your screening criteria before you take a fee. You may charge a reasonable fee, but say in writing before you take it what it covers (for example, the actual cost of a credit or reference check), whether any part is refundable, and how long the decision will take. Charge every applicant the same fee on the same terms: the federal Fair Housing Act reaches American Samoa and bars different terms because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin or disability. Because the Consumer Protection Act may reach a residential lease, don't take a fee for a unit you know is not available or for a check you don't run.

title: How Payments Are Applied in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets an order for applying a tenant's payment to rent, late fees, damages or other charges, so the lease governs. The shared clause `application-of-payments` applies each payment to rent first, which fits American Samoa's possession statute: a nonpayment case rests on unpaid rent after a written demand, and the demand must state the amount due. If you applied payments to fees first and then demanded possession for the resulting rent shortfall, a court could see the shortfall as fees, not rent. Without a lease term the common law of contracts decides (case law not searched); the cautious course is to follow any written direction the tenant gives with a payment and otherwise apply it to the oldest unpaid rent.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets, caps or bans a fee you may add for collecting past-due rent or damages, and no statute that lets a landlord recover attorney's fees in a rent or possession case; a possession judgment may award court costs. If you hand a debt to a collection agency, use one registered with the Office of Financial Institutions, which regulates collection agencies and requires them to register each year. Be cautious about adding a collection fee to the debt: American Samoa's usury law punishes anyone who extends credit and charges interest or fees above the legal rate, with forfeiture of the whole debt, and it is unsettled whether a fee added to overdue rent counts (case law not searched). The cautious course is to charge no collection fee unless the lease the tenant signed provides for it, to limit it to costs you actually pay a third party, and never to add it on top of interest on the same debt. A collection-fee term is lawful as far as we found, but this library does not offer one because of that forfeiture risk; if you want one, have a lawyer draft it for your lease.

title: Amounts Due at Signing in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that limits what you may collect when a lease is signed or begins: there is no cap on the security deposit, on first or last month's rent paid in advance, or on move-in fees, and no rule on when each must be paid. The lease decides, so list every amount due at signing and when it is due (`due-at-signing`), and give a written receipt for each. One federal rule reaches American Samoa: if a servicemember lawfully ends the lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, rent paid in advance for any period after the termination date must be refunded within 30 days of that date. Rent paid in advance is rent; if the tenant later falls behind, credit it as the lease says before you serve a demand for nonpayment.

title: No Fee-Disclosure Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires all-in rent pricing, a fee list on the lease's first page or in advertising, a set fee-disclosure sentence, or special terms for leases that renew automatically. The general Consumer Protection Act bars deceptive practices by a supplier, and a "supplier" includes a lessor; whether a residential lease counts as a consumer transaction under that Act is unsettled (case law not searched). The cautious course: state in the lease every fee the tenant must pay, with its amount or how it is figured and when it is due; don't advertise a rent figure that leaves out a fee every tenant must pay; and don't charge any fee the signed lease does not state.

title: Charging for Services Not Provided in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that is a landlord-specific ban on charging a tenant for services you don't provide. The Consumer Protection Act treats it as deceptive for a supplier to indicate that something has been supplied as promised when it has not, and a lessor can be a supplier; whether the Act reaches a residential lease is unsettled (case law not searched). So charge only for services you actually provide, as the lease describes them, and stop or credit a service fee when the service stops. If you pass water costs on to tenants, be careful: the water utility's rules put a multi-dwelling building on one meter unless you ask for a meter per unit, and make the applicant for that connection pay all its water charges, so build water into the rent, bill only the actual cost the lease describes, or have each unit metered in the tenant's name rather than marking it up.

title: Fees and Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no definition of rent and no statute that lets a lease turn fees into rent by calling them additional rent. The possession statute draws the line for you. The 7-day nonpayment ground speaks of "rent due" and excludes accelerated amounts owed because of a breach, while the written demand may also claim "other sums due under the lease" and must state the amount due. Whether late fees, utility charges or repair bills labelled additional rent count as rent due is unsettled (case law not searched). The cautious course: in a nonpayment demand, list unpaid rent separately from each other charge, and base the 7-day nonpayment case on rent alone; pursue unpaid fees as a lease breach (a termination demand that states the time to remedy) or as a money claim joined to the possession case. After a nonpayment judgment the tenant may still stop the writ by paying the judgment amount and costs.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no rental registration or rental licensing law, no city or county fee on rental units, and no statute that either allows or forbids having a tenant reimburse a government fee charged to you. The fee you are most likely to meet is territorial: no one may engage in business without a business licence, "business" covers any regular activity for gain, and the annual fee for a business not specially listed is $150; the Territorial Planning Commission decides how an activity is classified, so ask whether your rentals need a licence. If you rent housing to a guest worker, the law assumes you hold one: a host who charges a guest worker for housing must file a copy of the business licence and the written rent agreement with the guest worker's permit papers. That licence is a cost of your business, and the cautious course is to build it into the rent rather than bill it to tenants. If you want a tenant to reimburse a particular government charge, the lease must say so, name the charge and say how the amount is figured (case law not searched).

title: Government Fines and Abatement Costs in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that bars, caps or regulates passing a government fine on to a tenant, so the lease and the common law of contracts decide (case law not searched). One statute helps you: when the Department of Health orders a public health nuisance abated, an occupant or other person who caused or permitted the nuisance is liable to you for what you paid or what was assessed against the property, and unpaid abatement costs can be collected from rents by court order. Several health laws also put duties directly on lessees and occupants (rodent control, standing water and mosquitoes), so a tenant can be cited in their own name. For trash, the solid-waste rules treat you, as the person to whom rent is payable, as the "owner" who must set out refuse for the licensed collector, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise and notify the collector in writing, signed by both of you. Pass on only fines for conditions the tenant, household or guests caused, never a fine for a condition you are responsible for, and the optional clause `tenant-caused-fines-as` sets this out.

title: Late Fees in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that caps a residential late fee, requires a grace period, requires notice before a late fee is charged, or otherwise governs late fees on rent, so a late fee is owed only if the lease provides for it (`late-fee`). One set of rules may reach it: interest above 6% a year is unenforceable unless the debtor signed a written agreement, no one may charge more than 15% a year, and the usury law punishes anyone who extends credit and takes interest or fees above the legal rate, with forfeiture of the whole debt. Whether a late fee on rent counts as interest or such a fee is unsettled (case law not searched). The cautious course: put the late fee in the lease the tenant signs, keep it a modest one-time charge for each late payment that reflects your real cost of late payment, never charge a late fee and interest on the same late payment, and keep any interest clause at or below 15% a year. Keep late fees out of the rent figure in a nonpayment demand (`edu-fees-as-rent-as`). If you often accept late rent without objection, say in writing when you accept it that you are not waiving the due date (case law not searched).

title: No Statutory Late-Fee Cap in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that caps a residential late fee, sets a minimum grace period, limits how often a late fee may be charged, or requires notice before one is charged; the late-fee statutes we found cover government fees and utility bills, not rent. The limits that may apply come from the interest and usury laws (interest above 6% a year needs a signed writing and may never exceed 15% a year), and whether they reach a late fee is unsettled (case law not searched). See `edu-late-fee-as` for the cautious course.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires month-to-month tenants to get the same terms as fixed-term tenants, or that caps the rent difference between lease types, so you may price and draft each type differently. One law does draw a line between them: the emergency price-gouging rule reaches only rental housing leased on a month-to-month term, so from the declaration of a state of emergency until 30 days after the declaration (longer if the Governor extends it) you may not raise a month-to-month tenant's rent more than 10% above the rent charged just before the declaration, except for proven added costs (`edu-rent-control-as`). A fixed-term lease's rent is set by the lease for its term. Whatever the type, the same possession procedure, retaliation defence and post-judgment payment right apply.

title: Time Limits for Rent and Damage Claims in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa's general time limits for lawsuits apply to rent and damage claims. A suit on a written lease (for unpaid rent or other money the lease requires) must be brought within 10 years after the claim accrues; a suit on an oral lease, or for injury to the property, within 3 years; a suit to recover possession of real property within 20 years; and any claim with no stated period within 3 years. A contract claim is revived by the tenant's signed written admission that the debt is unpaid, or a like new promise to pay; the statute does not say a part payment alone revives it, so get a signed acknowledgment when a former tenant pays something toward an old balance. Whether each unpaid rent installment starts its own period is not settled by statute (case law not searched); the cautious course is to sue within 3 years for anything owed under an oral lease and well within 10 years under a written one. Remember that the possession case itself needs a fresh written demand.

title: No Rent-Concession Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that regulates rent concessions such as a free month, a move-in credit or reduced rent for the first months. You may offer them; write each one into the lease with its amount and the rental periods it covers (`rent-concession-wi`). Keep the Monthly Rent at the full amount and describe the concession as a credit, so that the rent stated in any later demand for nonpayment is clear. Don't advertise a concession you won't honor, since the Consumer Protection Act may reach a residential lease.

title: Rent Control in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no rent control, rent stabilization or rent registration, and no city or county governments that could adopt them, so you set the rent for a new tenancy and change it as the lease allows (`edu-rent-escalation-as`). The one limit on rent levels is the emergency price-gouging law. When the President or the Governor declares a state of emergency (for example after a cyclone or tsunami), from the declaration until 30 days after it, and for any further 30-day periods the Governor adds, you may not rent or offer to rent month-to-month housing for more than 10% above the rent you charged just before the declaration, unless you can prove the increase comes directly from added costs. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1,000 each and are a class A misdemeanor; the Attorney General enforces the law, and tenants have no private suit under it. The law's definition reaches only housing leased month to month, so a fixed-term lease's rent stays as the lease sets it. Village councils may have their own rules, which are not published; ask locally.

title: Rent for a Defective Unit in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that forbids demanding or collecting rent while a unit is cited as substandard. The possession statute protects the tenant another way: if you sue for possession for nonpayment, the court may not give you judgment if your own breach of the lease excuses the rent, and in any nonpayment judgment it deducts the part of the rent your breach excuses. No statute lets a lease waive this defence, so treat it as beyond the lease's reach (case law not searched). So if the unit has a serious defect you are responsible for under the lease, fix it before you demand full rent, or reduce the rent in writing while it lasts. If the Governor orders an unsafe building torn down, or the Department of Health orders a building closed or evacuated as a nuisance, don't collect rent for any period the tenant cannot lawfully live there. Whether the common law implies a duty to keep a dwelling habitable is unsettled (case law not searched).

title: Rent Changes During a Lease in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute regulates rent escalation clauses in a private lease, so during a fixed term the rent changes only as the lease provides: a schedule of new amounts or an index adjustment (`rent-escalation-la`), or an optional mid-term increase on 30 days' written notice with a right for the tenant to leave (`rent-increase-midterm-ky`). Without such a clause, the cautious course is to treat the rent as fixed for the term unless the tenant agrees in writing (case law not searched). Two limits apply. An increase imposed as a penalty for something the tenant lawfully did (such as complaining to the Department of Health) is a defence if you then try to end the tenancy for failure to pay it. And after a declared emergency the price-gouging law caps increases on month-to-month housing (`edu-rent-control-as`). If your building sits on government land, your own ground lease over 4 years must carry an inflation adjustment; that clause binds you, not your tenants.

title: Raising the Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets a notice period or form for raising the rent. During a fixed term you may raise the rent only as the lease provides (`edu-rent-escalation-as`). For a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy there is no rent-increase procedure in the Code: under the common law the change works by ending the current tenancy with proper notice and offering a new one at the new rent (case law not searched), so give the increase in writing at least one full rental period before it takes effect, and say the date and new amount. Two statutes limit what you may do. From the declaration of a state of emergency until 30 days after the declaration (and any 30-day extension the Governor orders), you may not raise the rent on month-to-month housing more than 10% above the pre-declaration rent, except for proven added costs (`edu-rent-control-as`). And an increase imposed as a penalty for a tenant's lawful act is a defence to a later possession case.

title: Paying Rent in Installments in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule on paying rent in installments or on whether scheduled installments are partial payments, so the lease may set any schedule (`rent-installments-or`). The possession statute's 7-day nonpayment ground speaks of rent due under the lease, so write each installment's amount and due date into the lease; a missed installment is then rent due on its own date, and your written demand can state it as the amount due (case law not searched). Give a receipt for each installment, and don't charge a late fee on an installment paid on its scheduled date.

title: Paying Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa law sets no default due date, place of payment or weekend rule for rent; those terms come from the lease (`rent-payment`), so state the amount, the due date and where and how to pay. Paying "without demand" in the lease does not change what you must do to recover possession: a nonpayment case still needs a written demand that states the amount due and is served as the statute requires (`edu-fees-as-rent-as`). Two statutes touch rent payment. If you house a guest worker for a charge, the rent must be set in a written agreement filed with the permit papers, and no host or sponsor may use coercion, duress or the threat of deportation to take wages beyond the agreed rent and reasonable household expenses (a class D felony). And a court protecting a domestic violence victim may order the abuser to pay the rent on the victim's home, so accept such payments. If the lease is silent, the common law decides when rent is due (case law not searched).

title: Rent Receipts in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, cash or otherwise, or that presumes earlier rent paid when a later receipt is shown. Give one anyway for every payment, and always for cash: a dated receipt naming the tenant, the premises, the amount, what it was for (rent for a named month, the deposit, a fee) and the balance is your best evidence of the amount due if you later serve a written demand. One rule applies to some rentals: if your building is an "apartment house", rooming house or lodging house and the occupant does not qualify for the permanent-resident exemption (a written lease of the unit for at least one month, plus conditions that must hold for the whole reporting quarter), the 5% hotel occupancy tax applies and must be shown separately on any receipt or invoice (`edu-rent-tax-as`).

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that creates a rent-reporting program, requires you to offer positive rent reporting, bars requiring a tenant to join one, or requires notice before you report late rent to a credit bureau. Federal credit-reporting law was not reviewed for this library and may apply if you report. If you do report, tell the tenant in the lease that you may, report only amounts actually owed, and correct any error promptly; the Consumer Protection Act may treat a misleading statement as deceptive if it reaches a residential lease.

title: Taxes on Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no sales or gross receipts tax on residential rent, but its hotel occupancy tax can reach residential rentals. The 5% tax applies to renting a room in any building where the public may obtain living quarters for a consideration, and the law names rooming houses, lodging houses and apartment houses. It does not apply to a permanent resident: a tenant who holds a written lease of the specific unit for at least one month, who occupied or had the right to occupy it for the whole reporting quarter, whose unit was not let on a non-lease basis during the quarter, and who did not sublet or assign it. So a written lease of a month or longer keeps an ordinary tenancy outside the tax only for a quarter in which every one of those conditions is met: a quarter in which the tenancy starts or ends part-way through, or in which the unit was also let on a short-stay basis, is taxed, and so are short stays and occupancies without a written lease in an apartment, rooming or lodging house. The tax is borne by the occupant: you must collect it with the rent, show it separately on the receipt or invoice, keep daily records, and file quarterly returns with the Treasury (late payment carries a 20% penalty plus interest). Whether a single house is an "apartment house" is not defined; ask the Treasury if you rent short-term. Your rental income is also subject to income tax, which this library does not cover.

title: Listing Fees in an American Samoa Lease
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease to list every fee, to state each fee's purpose, or to give notice before adding a fee later. List them anyway (`fees-and-charges-as`). Your right to any fee rests on the lease, so a charge the signed lease does not provide for is hard to collect; adding a fee during a fixed term needs the tenant's written agreement; any interest above 6% a year is unenforceable unless the tenant signed a written agreement to it; and the Consumer Protection Act, which may reach a residential lease, treats misleading statements by a lessor as deceptive. A clear list also lets your nonpayment demand separate rent from other charges.

title: Bounced Rent Payments in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that caps or sets the fee a landlord may charge for a bounced check or a failed electronic payment; the dishonored-check charges in the regulations ($5 to $25) apply only to payments to government offices. So a returned-payment fee is a matter of contract: put it in the lease (`returned-payments-as`) and keep it close to what your bank actually charges you plus a modest handling cost. The lease may also require a replacement payment by cashier's check or money order, and certified funds after repeated failures. Separately, passing a bad check with intent to defraud is a crime. If a check bounced for insufficient funds or credit, you send the tenant written notice of that by first-class mail to the address on the check or the tenant's last known address, and the check is not made good within 10 days, that failure is evidence of intent to defraud (a check on an account that did not exist is evidence of it without notice); send that notice whether or not you involve the police. A bounced rent check leaves the rent unpaid, so serve the written demand if you intend to seek possession.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that delays rent, waives late fees or pauses possession cases for federal or American Samoa Government employees or contractors affected by a government shutdown or a lapse in appropriations. The lease's ordinary rent, late-fee and default terms apply. Consider a written payment plan for an affected tenant. If you do seek possession, the statute's protections still apply: a written demand and 7 days after service before a nonpayment case, and the tenant's right to stop the writ by paying the judgment amount and costs.

title: American Samoa Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: American Samoa law sets few money limits on a residential lease. No statute caps the security deposit, move-in money, the late fee, an application fee, a returned-payment fee or an ordinary rent increase, and none requires a grace period. The limits that do exist: (1) Interest: interest above 6% a year is unenforceable unless the tenant signed a written agreement to it, 15% a year is the ceiling, and 6% is presumed on overdue debts with no written rate; whether a late fee counts as interest is unsettled (`edu-late-fee-as`). (2) Emergencies: from a declared state of emergency until 30 days after the declaration (plus any extension), month-to-month rent may not rise more than 10% above the pre-declaration rent (`edu-rent-control-as`). (3) Hotel occupancy tax: 5% on occupancies in apartment, rooming or lodging houses, except a tenant with a written lease of a month or more who meets the exemption's conditions for the whole reporting quarter (`edu-rent-tax-as`). (4) Possession timing: 7 days after a served written demand before a nonpayment case, and in most cases 10 days after judgment before the writ issues, during which the tenant may pay the judgment amount and costs.

title: No Rule on Prorating Subsidized Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets a formula for reducing a subsidized tenant's share, or the housing agency's share, of rent when part of a unit is unfit. The American Samoa Economic Development Authority is the territory's public housing agency under federal housing law, and the program's own rules and your contract with the agency govern any abatement of its payment (not reviewed for this library). The general rule applies to every tenant: in a nonpayment case the court deducts whatever part of the rent your breach of the lease excuses, and that breach is a defence to possession. So if part of a subsidized unit becomes unusable through no fault of the tenant, agree a written reduction of the tenant's share for the period, tell the agency, and don't demand the full tenant share until the unit is restored.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that addresses late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent. A late fee rests on the tenant's own delay, so charge it only on the tenant's share, never because the housing agency paid its share late, and write the late-fee clause that way. The federal CARES Act's ban on such fees ran only during its 2020 moratorium. Program rules and your agency contract may limit fees further (not reviewed for this library), and the general late-fee cautions apply (`edu-late-fee-as`).

title: No Property Tax to Pass Through in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no real property tax: our searches of the Code, the regulations and the uncompiled laws found none, so there is no property tax increase to pass on to a tenant, and the library's tax-escalation clause does not fit. If you want a tenant to share an increase in your property insurance premium, no American Samoa statute addresses it; the lease must say so expressly and state the tenant's share and how you will prove the increase (case law not searched). The hotel occupancy tax, where it applies, is a separate tax on the occupant (`edu-rent-tax-as`).

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa law gives you interest on unpaid rent and other amounts without any lease clause: where there is no written agreement on a rate, interest at 6% a year is presumed on overdue debts, and courts have used 6% for judgments (a lead from the Bar's case notes; case law not searched). A higher rate needs a written agreement signed by the tenant, and no one may charge more than 15% a year; charging more is usury, a crime that also forfeits the whole debt. So a signed lease may set a rate up to that ceiling (`interest-on-unpaid-amounts-as`), but keep it well below it, apply it only to amounts that stay unpaid after the due date, and never charge interest and a late fee on the same late payment, since whether a late fee counts as interest is unsettled (`edu-late-fee-as`). For damages whose amount is disputed (for example, repair costs after move-out), interest is safest claimed from the date you gave the tenant a written statement of the amount (case law not searched).

title: No Security Deposit Cap in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that caps a residential security deposit, sets a different limit by tenancy type, or limits a separate pet or furniture deposit. You may set the deposit in the lease (the library's clauses use the security-deposit fill-in). The lease and the common law govern how it is held, used and returned (case law not searched), so state in the lease what the deposit secures, what you may deduct (unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition), and when and how you will return it with an itemized list. One federal rule applies: knowingly holding the deposit of a servicemember who lawfully ends the lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, to cover rent for the period after termination, is a federal misdemeanor.

title: Holding a Security Deposit in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that tells a landlord where or how to hold a tenant's security deposit: no trust or escrow account, no bar on mixing it with your own funds, no bond and no notice of the bank. The lease decides. The cautious course is to keep deposits in a separate bank account in American Samoa, record each tenant's deposit, and say in the lease that the deposit remains the tenant's money held as security, so that it is easy to account for and to hand to a buyer if you sell (`edu-no-deposit-sale-rule-as`).

title: No Interest on Security Deposits in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to pay interest on a residential security deposit or to put it in an interest-bearing account. The only deposit-interest rules found concern banks; the power and water utility rules, for example, require customer deposits but say nothing about interest on them. So unless the lease promises interest, none is owed on a deposit you return on time. If you keep a deposit past the time the lease allows, the tenant may claim interest on it as an overdue debt at the 6% legal rate (`edu-unpaid-amount-interest-as`; case law not searched).

title: No Deposit Non-Waiver Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: Because American Samoa has no security deposit statute, there is no statutory deposit right for a lease to waive and no rule that voids a waiver. We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule on waiving deposit rights. The tenant's claim to the deposit rests on the lease and the common law (case law not searched). The cautious course is still not to include a clause that forfeits the whole deposit on any breach or waives the tenant's right to an accounting: a court may treat it as a penalty, and the Consumer Protection Act may reach grossly one-sided lease terms. Possession protections in the statute are a different matter: no statute lets a lease waive them, so treat them as beyond the lease's reach (`edu-nonwaivable-rights-as`).

title: Deposits When You Sell in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that says what happens to tenants' security deposits when a rental property is sold, or that releases the seller once deposits are transferred. The common law and the sale contract decide (case law not searched). The cautious course: in the sale contract, transfer each deposit (or credit it to the buyer) and have the buyer assume the duty to return it; then tell each tenant in writing the buyer's name and address and the deposit amount transferred, and keep a copy. A registered lease gives notice of its terms to everyone who later deals with the land, which is one more reason to register written leases with the Territorial Registrar.

title: Holding Deposits in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule on a holding deposit or other money taken to reserve a unit before the lease is signed: no cap, no refund deadline and no rule doubling it if you back out. The agreement you make with the applicant decides, read with the common law of contracts (case law not searched). Put the terms in writing before you take the money: the amount, how long you will hold the unit, that it becomes part of the first month's rent or the deposit if the lease is signed, when it is refunded (for example, if you decline the applicant or don't offer the lease), and what part, if any, you may keep if the applicant backs out. Take the same terms from every applicant, since the federal Fair Housing Act reaches American Samoa.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that bars a nonrefundable deposit or fee, or that requires a particular notice before you charge one. Your right to keep money rests on the lease, so if any payment (a pet fee, a cleaning fee) is meant to be nonrefundable, the lease must say so and name the amount (`nonrefundable-fees-wv`); anything else you take as security for the tenant's performance should be treated as part of the refundable deposit. Don't call a payment a "deposit" if you mean to keep it: a deposit is ordinarily returned less proper deductions, and the Consumer Protection Act may treat a misleading label as deceptive if it reaches a residential lease (case law not searched).

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Fees in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a separate written notice, a separate signature or particular wording for a nonrefundable fee or deposit. State any nonrefundable amount in the lease itself, with its amount and purpose (`edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-as`).

title: No Fee-in-Lieu-of-Deposit Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that authorizes, bans or regulates a fee charged in place of a security deposit, or a deposit-replacement insurance or surety product. If you offer one, write in the lease that it is optional, that the tenant may pay an ordinary deposit instead, that the fee is not a deposit and is not refunded, and that the tenant still owes you for damage and unpaid rent. Insurance products sold in the territory are regulated under the insurance title, which this library does not cover, so check with the provider that it is authorized to do business in American Samoa.

title: No Deposit Installment Right in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or that limits doing so. You may agree to it: write the installment amounts and due dates into the lease, and say that an unpaid installment is a sum due under the lease. Keep deposit installments separate from rent in your records, because the 7-day nonpayment ground speaks of rent due, and a missed deposit installment is safer treated as a lease breach (`edu-fees-as-rent-as`).

title: Deposits and Last Month's Rent in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that limits taking last month's rent in advance, or that lets or bars a tenant applying the security deposit to the last month's rent. The lease decides. If you want the deposit to stay available for damage, say in the lease that the tenant may not use it as rent; if you collect last month's rent in advance, label it as prepaid rent (not a deposit) and credit it to the last rental period. If a servicemember lawfully ends the lease early under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, rent paid in advance for any period after the termination date must be refunded within 30 days.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition report or inventory, or a notice about one. Do one anyway: because the deposit and any damage claim rest on the lease and the common law (case law not searched), a dated condition report signed by you and the tenant at move-in, with photographs, is your best evidence of what changed. The optional clause `move-in-condition-report-as` sets this up. Offer the tenant a walk-through at move-out and give a written list of any damage you charge against the deposit.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a notice of a move-in or move-out inspection, or that penalizes a landlord, for example by forfeiting the right to deduct from the deposit, for failing to give one. The cautious practice is still to offer joint inspections in writing and keep a signed condition report (`edu-no-condition-inspection-rule-as`).

title: No Rule on Pre-Set Deposit Charges in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that permits, limits or requires notice of a schedule of pre-set charges (such as carpet cleaning or repainting) to be taken from a security deposit. If you use one, put it in the lease, keep each charge close to what the work actually costs, and charge only for work actually done beyond normal wear and tear; a fixed charge unrelated to real damage risks being treated as a penalty under the common law (case law not searched).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no unclaimed-property act that makes a landlord report deposit refunds, but its escheat law reaches any personal property, including money owed, whose owner has been unknown or unlocated, or which has gone unclaimed, for 14 successive years; such property escheats to the Territory through an action the Attorney General brings in the High Court. We found no rule that lets a landlord keep a deposit refund the tenant does not collect, and no rule that bars a lease clause saying so. So send the refund and itemized statement to the tenant's forwarding or last known address, keep proof, and hold any unclaimed refund in your records as money owed to the tenant; don't write a lease clause that forfeits an unclaimed refund to you, which could be challenged as a penalty (case law not searched).

title: No Surrender or Forwarding-Address Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that requires a tenant to give a forwarding address, requires you to give notice when the tenant surrenders the unit, or starts a deposit-return clock on surrender. The lease decides, so ask in the lease for a forwarding address at move-out, say when the deposit and an itemized statement will be returned (a short period such as 30 days is the cautious choice), and send them to the forwarding address or, without one, to the last address you have, keeping proof of mailing.

title: No Expedited Deposit Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets a deposit-return deadline at all, or a faster or slower one for particular situations such as abandonment, early termination, eviction or a tenant's death. The lease and the common law decide (case law not searched). Return the deposit and an itemized statement within the period the lease states, measured from the day you get possession back, and if the tenant has died, pay it to the personal representative or as the probate court directs.

title: Deposits After Domestic Violence in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa law gives a domestic violence victim no statutory right to end a lease early, so there is no special deposit clock after such a termination; we found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule on it. What does apply: a court's order for protection may remove the abuser from the residence regardless of who owns it, may order the abuser to pay the rent, and may order the abuser to pay for repair or replacement of damaged property. So comply with any order, accept rent paid under it, and if you agree to let a victim leave early, return the deposit on the lease's ordinary terms once all occupants have left, charging damage the abuser caused to the abuser rather than to the victim where you can. In federally assisted housing, federal VAWA protections also apply.

title: Furnished Rentals in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that sets special rules for furnished rentals, a separate furniture deposit or a furniture inventory. Use the optional `furnishings-included-la` clause to list the items and their condition, and include them in the move-in condition report. One rule can turn on how you rent: if you let furnished rooms or units short-term in a rooming, lodging or apartment house, the 5% hotel occupancy tax applies unless the occupant holds a written lease of at least one month and meets the exemption's other conditions for the whole reporting quarter (`edu-rent-tax-as`).

title: No Territorial Deposit Penalty; One Federal Offence
bodyText: American Samoa has no security-deposit statute, so no territorial law sets a penalty, such as double or triple damages or loss of your right to withhold, for mishandling a deposit. We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule on deposit penalties. A tenant who says you kept too much can sue for the balance under the lease and the general contract law the territory applies (case law not searched). If the territory's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases, which is unsettled, a deceptive deposit practice could also cost you the tenant's actual damages or $100, whichever is greater. One federal rule does reach American Samoa: when a servicemember or dependent lawfully ends a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, knowingly holding their security deposit or belongings to cover rent for the period after termination is a federal crime (a fine, up to one year in prison, or both). Return the deposit promptly with a written list of deductions and keep only what the lease allows.

title: No Deposit-Return Deadline in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule sets a deadline for returning a security deposit, requires an itemized statement of deductions, or makes the tenant give a forwarding address; we found none. Your lease sets those terms, so use the library's American Samoa return clause (`security-deposit-return-as`), which states your own deadline and promises an itemized list. Keep only what the lease allows and return the rest promptly; a tenant can sue for money wrongly kept under the general contract law the territory applies (case law not searched). If a servicemember ends the lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, federal law requires you to refund rent paid in advance for the period after termination within 30 days of the termination date, and holding the deposit to cover rent after that date is a federal crime (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-as`).

title: No Deposit-Standards Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires you to post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if different tenants pay different deposits, and none caps the deposit or says how it must be held (no separate-account or interest rule); we found none. The federal Fair Housing Act does reach American Samoa: unless one of its exemptions applies, you may not set a different deposit or other rental term because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Use the same written criteria for every applicant (for example, credit history or a pet) and keep a note of why each deposit was set.

title: Using the Security Deposit in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule lists what a security deposit may be used for or limits its amount; your lease decides, and we found no rule on the subject. The shared clause (`security-deposit-use`) lets you apply the deposit to unpaid rent and other defaults and to damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and not to wear and tear or pre-existing damage; that fits the general contract law the territory applies (case law not searched), so use it as written. Say in the lease that the deposit is not the last month's rent unless you intend it to be. If a servicemember ends the lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, federal law lets you charge reasonable charges for excess wear but no early-termination charge.

title: Utility Deposits in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa law governs a utility deposit that you, as landlord, collect from a tenant; we found no such rule. If you take money to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease, treat it as part of the security deposit: say in the lease what it secures, and return any balance with an itemized statement. The utility rules do cover deposits the Power Authority takes from its own customers. For electricity, a deposit is required from residential and most other customers in the amount the fee schedule sets (currently $75 for a residential account), it may be increased for a customer to protect the utility, and the utility reviews deposits and may refund one when the customer's credit is satisfactory. For water, an applicant pays the necessary deposits, but the rules set no amount or refund terms, and a customer who has been disconnected may be required to pay an additional deposit or pay in advance. If the tenant opens the account in their own name, that deposit is between the tenant and the utility, but you must co-sign the application and answer for the tenant's past-due bills; if you hold the account, for example one water connection serving several units you manage, you pay the deposit and answer for all water supplied through it.

title: Tenant Alterations in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule governs whether a tenant may alter, improve or install anything in a rental home, or who owns the result; we found none. The lease decides, so the shared Alterations clause (`no-alterations`) and, if you want it, the optional improvements-ownership clause (`improvements-ownership-la`) work as written. Without a lease term, ownership of things a tenant attaches turns on the common law of fixtures (case law not searched), so put your rule in the lease. The federal Fair Housing Act reaches American Samoa: you may not refuse a tenant with a disability permission to make reasonable modifications, at the tenant's expense, that are needed for full enjoyment of the home, though in a rental you may, where reasonable, make permission conditional on the tenant restoring the interior at the end, reasonable wear and tear excepted. A building put up in violation of the territory's building law must be removed or altered at the owner's expense on the Governor's order, so don't let a tenant build or add a structure without your written consent and the required approval.

title: Bed Bugs and Pests in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule deals with bed bugs, sets inspection or treatment deadlines, splits treatment costs or spells out a tenant's duty to cooperate; we found none, so you may use the optional pest-cooperation clause (`pest-cooperation-pr`) as written. One territorial rule covers rodents and binds both you and your tenant: every owner, lessee or occupant of an occupied building must take adequate good-faith measures to eradicate rodents, keep the building and the spaces around it free of food and garbage that could feed or shelter them, and stack firewood, lumber and loose materials in an orderly way. The Director of Health may inspect buildings at reasonable hours and order a public health nuisance (anything that endangers life or health) abated. If the Department of Health abates a nuisance and charges the cost to the property, an occupant who caused or permitted it is liable to you for what you paid. Respond to infestation reports promptly and keep records of treatment.

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule says whether a lease may require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and the territory has no security-deposit statute setting what may be deducted; we found none. The optional carpet-cleaning clause (`carpet-cleaning-ar`) may be used as written. Keep its condition that the carpets were professionally cleaned just before the tenancy, so the charge reflects the tenant's use rather than ordinary wear, and deduct only the reasonable cost you actually pay, listed in your itemized deposit statement (`security-deposit-return-as`). Whether a charge for ordinary wear could be recovered rests on the lease and the common law the territory applies (case law not searched), so don't charge for it.

title: Cold-Weather Vacate Notice: Not Applicable in American Samoa
bodyText: Not applicable in American Samoa. The territory has a tropical climate with no freezing season, and no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires a tenant to give notice or take freeze precautions before vacating or leaving a home empty; we found none. If you want to know when a tenant will be away for a long stretch, put an absence-notice term in the lease (`edu-no-extended-absence-notice-as`).

title: No Construction-Lien Law in American Samoa
bodyText: We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule giving contractors, suppliers or workers a lien on real property for construction or repair work; the territory has no mechanics' lien law. A contractor your tenant hires therefore has no statutory lien on your property; its claim is a contract claim against whoever hired it, and any other theory against you would rest on the common law (case law not searched). You may still use the optional no-liens clause (`no-liens-ar`) as written: it makes the tenant pay everyone it hires, tell contractors that you are not responsible, and cover your costs if a claim reaches you. Two related rules: a house on communal land that has been separated from the land by a recorded agreement can be made subject to a lien as if it were personal property, and the Department of Health can charge its nuisance-abatement costs as a lien on the property (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-as`).

title: Disturbing Neighbors in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa landlord-tenant statute makes a tenant keep the peace, so the shared Disturbance clause (`no-disturbance`) is what creates that duty in the lease; use it as written. The criminal law backs it up. Making unreasonable noise, fighting, or violent or threatening behavior with intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance or alarm, or recklessly risking it, is public peace disturbance, a class B misdemeanor; threatening a crime or fighting on private property so as to purposely alarm others there is private peace disturbance. A person who keeps a public health nuisance (anything that endangers life or health) on property he owns or occupies after 10 days' written notice to abate commits a misdemeanor. To end a tenancy over disturbances, use the lease's termination power and the court's summary repossession procedure with a written demand, never self-help. Village councils keep their own customary rules, which are not published and may cover noise or conduct; ask the village if your property is in one.

title: Recording Move-In Condition in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires a move-in inspection, checklist or condition statement, or says what a tenant's signed acknowledgment of condition does; we found none, so the shared Existing Condition clause (`existing-condition`) works as written. Record the condition anyway, with a signed checklist and dated photos: with no deposit statute, the lease and that record are your only proof of what damage the tenant caused (`edu-security-deposit-use-as`). A signed acknowledgment does not make an unsafe home lawful: every completed building must be inspected by the Department of Public Works to determine whether it is safe for occupancy, and a building in such a dilapidated condition as to be unsafe and dangerous must be torn down within 30 days after the Governor's written notice. For homes built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure applies at signing (`lead-based-paint`).

title: No Absence-Notice Rule in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, requires the lease to contain such a term, or gives you a right to enter while the tenant is away; we found none. The shared absence-notice clause (`extended-absence-notice-ks`) may be used as a lease term; any damages for a willful failure to give notice are ordinary contract damages (case law not searched). A notice term helps you tell a trip from an abandonment, but it does not let you retake the home: possession comes back only through a court case (normally the summary repossession procedure), and entry must be permitted by law and peaceable. While a building stands unoccupied, its owner or lessee must keep it and its grounds free of rubbish and keep weeds and grass down.

title: Child Care in a Rented Home
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, or sets conditions such as liability waivers or insurance; we found none, so the lease may forbid or condition it (see `residential-use-only`). We also found no published child-care licensing rule in the territory's code or regulations, though two statutes refer to licensed child day care, so ask the Department of Health or Human and Social Services before you allow one. If a tenant does run one, the territory's smoking ban follows it: a private residence used as a licensed day care center is a public place, and one used as a child care facility is a place of employment, so smoking is banned in its enclosed areas. Caring for others' children for gain is likely a business that needs a business license, and zoning limits a home occupation to one with no other person employed (`edu-home-business-as`). Check your insurance before agreeing.

title: Home Businesses in an American Samoa Rental
bodyText: No American Samoa statute makes a home-based business a use a lease cannot restrict, so the shared Residential Use Only clause (`residential-use-only`) may forbid or limit business use, and you may allow a specific business in writing; we found no rule to the contrary. Zoning permits a home occupation as an accessory use in single-dwelling, multiple-dwelling and agricultural zones, but only an occupation carried on by occupants of the dwelling as a secondary use, with no display, stock-in-trade or commodity sold on the premises and no other person employed. No one may engage in business in American Samoa without a business license unless exempt, and failing to get one is a class B misdemeanor, so ask a tenant who runs a business from the home to show you the license. A home occupation needs one parking space beyond what the residence requires.

title: Co-Tenant Liability in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule says whether co-tenants are jointly and severally liable under a lease, or whether accepting one co-tenant's share of the rent releases that co-tenant; we found none. The shared Joint Liability clause (`joint-liability`) supplies the term and works as written; without it, the answer turns on the common law of contracts the territory applies (case law not searched). One federal rule: when a servicemember lawfully ends a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, the termination also ends any obligation of the servicemember's dependent under that lease, so plan for that when a servicemember signs with a spouse.

title: Yard Care and Watering in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule assigns lawn, yard or irrigation work between landlord and tenant, or requires a separate signed writing for it, so the lease decides and the shared Landscaping clause (`landscaping-irrigation`) works as written. Several territorial duties fall on whoever owns, leases or occupies the land, so both of you are covered. Every owner, lessee or occupant of an occupied building must keep weeds and grass near the building, out to the road, cut so they do not shelter rodents (in rural or village areas only up to the property line). Every person who owns or possesses land must keep it free of rotten wood, decayed logs and stumps, heaps of coconut husks and rotting grass or leaves. Owners and users of land must destroy declared noxious weeds as soon as they find them. The water utility may cut off service where water is wastefully or negligently used and significantly affects the general service, if the waste is not corrected within five days of its written notice, and taking a large quantity of water needs its arrangement first. Say in the lease who does each task.

title: No Utility Lien for a Tenant's Unpaid Bill in American Samoa
bodyText: Power, water and wastewater service in American Samoa is supplied by the American Samoa Power Authority, not by a city. We found no American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule that makes a tenant's unpaid power, water, sewer or garbage bill a lien on your property. But the Authority's rules make you answer for it another way: for rented property the landlord or owner must co-sign the tenant's application or account transfer, co-signers are financially responsible for the tenant's past-due bills, and service is not restored until they are paid or put on a payment plan. If you take water for several units through one connection, you pay all water supplied through it. Separately, if the Department of Health abates a public health nuisance on your property and is not repaid, it may assess the cost as a lien on the property or collect it from the rents under a court order, and an occupant who caused or permitted the nuisance is liable to you for what you pay. Have tenants put utilities in their own names where the meters allow (`edu-utilities-responsibility-as`), have the lease require them to keep the accounts current and repay anything you pay as co-signer (the optional clause `utility-cosigner-reimbursement-as` does this), and check the account with the Authority at move-out.

title: Occupancy Limits in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute or regulation sets a maximum number of people who may live in a private rental home or gives neighbors a right to enforce one; we found none. The territory adopted the 1964 Uniform Building Code, Short Form, and amended its table of available square feet per occupant to 100 square feet for dwellings; the code book itself is not in the sources we searched, so we could not confirm how that figure applies to the number of people living in a home. The federal Fair Housing Act reaches American Samoa: it leaves reasonable government limits on the number of occupants in place, but bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because a household has children, and a limit you set yourself is judged under that rule (federal guidance and case law not searched). List every occupant in the lease (`permitted-occupants`), apply the same reasonable limit to every applicant, and base it on the home's size and bedrooms.

title: Acts the Law Forbids Tenants in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no statutory list of acts a residential tenant must not do, so the shared Prohibited Acts clause (`prohibited-acts-renter-wy`) is what puts them in the lease; use it as written. Several criminal laws back it up, because your property is property of another as far as the tenant is concerned. Knowingly damaging it is property damage (a felony above $1,000), tampering with or making a connection to utility property is a crime, and the Power Authority's own rules forbid tampering with its meters and connections and make it unlawful for a customer to resell electricity. Gambling is a crime, including knowingly letting a place be used for it, and a room or building regularly used for prostitution is a public nuisance whose owner can be barred from using or occupying it for up to a year if the owner knew or had reason to believe what was going on. Possessing a controlled substance, including marijuana, is a felony. Act promptly on reports and enforce the lease through the court's summary repossession procedure, not self-help.

title: Residential Use Only in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute says what happens when a tenant uses a home for a purpose other than the one it was let for, so the shared Residential Use Only clause (`residential-use-only`) works as a lease covenant; we found no statutory remedy. Enforce it through the lease's own termination power: once you end the lease under that power, a tenant who holds over can be removed through the court's summary repossession procedure after a written demand (`edu-prohibited-acts-renter-as`). Zoning backs the clause: no building or land may be used for a purpose its zone does not permit, and a home occupation is allowed only as a secondary use by the occupants with no stock sold on the premises and no outside employee (`edu-home-business-as`). Some uses are crimes in themselves, such as gambling or using the home for prostitution.

title: Smoking Rules for American Samoa Rentals
bodyText: American Samoa's smoke-free law bans smoking in enclosed areas of public places and places of employment, but a private residence is not a public place unless it is used as a licensed day care center, and not a place of employment unless it is used as a child care, adult day care or health care facility. So smoking inside a rented home is governed by the lease, and the shared Smoking Policy clause (`smoking-policy`) works as written. Lobbies and other parts of a building that are used by and open to the public are public places; whether the shared hallways of an apartment building count is unsettled (case law not searched), so ban smoking in enclosed common areas. As owner, or the lessee or manager in charge of regulated space, make every reasonable effort to prevent smoking there by posting signs at each entrance. The law's definition of smoking covers lit tobacco and similar products, not e-cigarettes, so a vaping ban rests on the lease. Marijuana has no protection: possessing it is a felony.

title: Subletting and Assignment in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule requires you to consent to a sublease or assignment or limits your reasons for refusing, so a lease may require your prior written consent in your sole discretion, as the shared clause (`no-sublet-assign`) does; we found no rule to the contrary. One court rule helps you: in a summary repossession case, anyone who becomes a subtenant of the premises after service of the notice the rules provide for is bound by the judgment (the rule does not say whether that is the demand or the summons, so serve both promptly). Land status matters. A lease of communal (native) land has no validity until the Governor approves it in writing, and a sublease or assignment of it is a further disposal of an interest in native land, so treat it as needing the same approval unless your lawyer advises otherwise (case law not searched). A sublease or assignment in writing is an instrument that does not pass an interest in the land until registered with the Territorial Registrar.

title: Tenant Forwarding Legal Papers in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule makes a tenant tell you about, or forward, papers in a proceeding against the property, and none deals with attornment (a tenant agreeing to recognize someone else as landlord); we found none. The shared forwarding clause (`tenant-forward-proceedings-ca`) is worth using, for two reasons. All controversies relating to land, including actions to evict persons or remove structures from land, belong to the Land and Titles Division of the High Court, so a family or neighbor claiming the land may sue the person in possession, your tenant, and you may not hear of it unless the tenant tells you. And in a summary repossession case, anyone who becomes a subtenant after service of the notice the rules provide for (the rule does not say whether that is the demand or the summons) is bound by the judgment.

title: Tenant Insurance and Claims in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule says whether you may require a tenant to carry renter's insurance, to make a claim on the tenant's own policy, or to name you on it, and none governs subrogation between you and the tenant's insurer; we found none. A lease requirement to carry insurance is a matter of contract. Don't use the tenant's policy as a substitute for your own: insure the building yourself, and treat the tenant's insurance as covering the tenant's belongings and liability. If the Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases, which is unsettled, a misleading description of what the tenant's insurance must cover could expose you to a claim, so describe the requirement plainly.

title: Tenant Upkeep Duties in American Samoa
bodyText: American Samoa has no landlord-tenant act listing a tenant's upkeep duties, so the shared Tenant Maintenance clause (`tenant-maintenance`) is what puts them in the lease; use it as written. Several territorial rules bind the tenant directly as occupant. Every owner, lessee or occupant of an occupied building must keep garbage, rubbish and filth from accumulating in or near the building, keep the surroundings free of food and harborage for rodents, and act in good faith against an infestation. No one may let solid waste accumulate on property he owns, leases or possesses. On the water side, the customer is responsible for maintenance and repairs of pipes and fixtures beyond the meter. Note that putting garbage out for collection is your duty as the person to whom rent is paid unless you and the tenant agree otherwise and both sign a notice to the collector (`garbage-setout-as`). If a tenant willfully or negligently creates a serious and continuing health hazard or extensive and continuing physical damage, you may serve a written demand and recover possession if it is not put right within 7 days.

title: Tenant Repair Agreements in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute, regulation or court rule authorizes, limits or sets formalities for an agreement that a tenant will do repairs, maintenance or minor remodeling, and none requires a separate signed writing or something given in return; we found none. The optional repair-agreement clause (`tenant-repair-agreement-hi`) may be used as written: list each task specifically and state what the tenant gets for it. Two limits remain. An agreement between you and the tenant does not take you out of the duties the law puts on every owner, lessee or occupant (for example the rodent and garbage duties), because those bind each of you. The one duty the rules let you hand over by agreement is putting garbage out for collection, and only with a notice to the collector signed by both of you (`garbage-setout-as`). Whether a court would enforce an agreement that leaves the home unfit rests on the common law (case law not searched).

title: Tenant Duties Under American Samoa Law
bodyText: American Samoa has no landlord-tenant act listing tenant duties, but several laws bind tenants directly whatever the lease says. (1) Sanitation: every owner, lessee or occupant must keep garbage and filth from accumulating in or near the building, keep weeds and grass down and act against rodents; no one may let solid waste accumulate on property he leases or possesses; anyone who owns or possesses land must keep it clear of rotten wood, stumps and husk heaps; and keeping a public health nuisance after 10 days' written notice is a crime. (2) Property: knowingly damaging property of another, which includes your property, is a crime, as is tampering with utility property; a utility customer may not resell electricity. (3) Conduct: unreasonable noise and fighting are peace-disturbance crimes, and gambling and drug possession are crimes. (4) Possession: a tenant who creates a serious and continuing health hazard or extensive and continuing physical damage may be removed if it is not put right within 7 days after your written demand. The lease clauses on maintenance, conduct and use repeat these duties as contract terms (`edu-tenant-maintenance-as`, `edu-prohibited-acts-renter-as`, `edu-disturbance-as`).

title: Who Pays Utilities in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute says whether landlord or tenant pays for utilities, so the lease decides and the shared Utilities clause (`utilities-responsibility`) works as written; the American Samoa Power Authority supplies electricity, water and wastewater service, and every water customer also has, and pays for, wastewater service. The utility's rules shape what you can do. For electricity, when a building is occupied by several customers, each becomes a customer of the utility with its own meter. The customer whose meter it is pays for the power it registers until it ends service in writing and the utility finally terminates it. For water, a building gets one delivery point, and a building with several units is on one meter unless the owner asks, at its own expense, for a meter per unit, grouped at one central point. Several units under one management may be served by separate meters or by one connection, and with one connection the applicant must pay for all water supplied. For rented property, for electricity and water alike, the landlord must co-sign the tenant's application or account transfer, and the co-signer answers for the tenant's past-due bills. Equipment between the water meter and the outlets is the customer's responsibility, not the utility's. Garbage set-out is your duty as the person to whom rent is paid unless you shift it to the tenant (`garbage-setout-as`). Unpaid bills are the customer's and the co-signer's debt, and service is not restored until past-due accounts are paid or put on a payment plan (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-as`). These rules come from the Power Authority's rules as printed in the 2024 Administrative Code; its board may adjust rates and fees by resolution, so check current charges with the Authority.

title: Submetering and Service Interruptions in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute or regulation sets a regime for electricity or water that a landlord submeters and bills to tenants, or for interrupting such service; we found none. Be careful before you submeter electricity: reselling electricity received from the utility is unlawful, a customer may not supply another person or premises through its service without the Power Authority's approval, and in a building with several tenants the electric rules give each tenant its own meter as a customer of the utility; whether recharging tenants for electricity by submeter counts as resale is unsettled (case law not searched), so the cautious course is separate utility meters. The current water rules have no resale ban, and water for several units may come through one connection in your name, so recharging tenants for water rests on the lease; state the method in it. Never interrupt a tenant's service to force payment or possession: possession comes back only through the courts, and tampering with utility property or another's property is a crime. The statute requiring 10 working days' notice before a public utility cuts off a delinquent consumer defines a public utility broadly enough that a landlord supplying power or water to tenants might be covered (unsettled), which is one more reason not to do it.

title: Proof of Utility Payment in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute or regulation gives you a right to proof that a tenant has paid utilities, or limits a lease term requiring it, so the shared clause (`utility-payment-evidence`) works as a contract term; we found no rule on the subject. It matters even when the account is in the tenant's name: the Power Authority's rules make you co-sign the tenant's application or account transfer and hold you responsible for the tenant's past-due bills. Where an account stays in your name, an electric customer remains responsible for the power registered on its meter until it ends service in writing and the utility finally terminates it, and a water account for several units on one connection is the applicant's responsibility. Default on any amount counts as a default on all of a customer's services, and the utility may cut off service at all of its locations. Ask for proof on a schedule, and when a tenant leaves, close or transfer accounts in writing.

title: Keeping Utilities On in American Samoa
bodyText: No American Samoa statute makes a tenant keep utility service connected, so the shared clause (`utility-service-continuity`) works as a contract term; use it as written. The cut-off rules a tenant's account is subject to: a public utility may not terminate service to a consumer whose account is not delinquent without consent, and before terminating a delinquent account must send notice by first-class mail or post it on the structure, stating that service will end after 10 working days; a utility that terminates in violation must credit the consumer $25 plus $10 for each full day without service.
